characters.name: Dani
characters.description: A former teacher from America who moved to London and took up the position of au pair for the Wingrave children. Adaptational Heroism:The Turn of the Screwleft it ambiguous as to whether there ever truly was a ghostly threat to the children, or if the governess was losing her mind andshewas the real threat. Here, Dani, although haunted by her past, is of sound mind, the ghosts are definitely real and a threat to the children,and Dani ultimately saves not only Miles and Flora, but every ghost trapped in Bly Manor. Adaptational Job Change: Downplayed. InThe Turn of the Screwthe protagonist is a governess, while here Dani is specifically an au pair (or nanny), which is more fitting for theSetting Updatefrom the 19th century to 1987. Adaptational Nationality: The governess inThe Turn of the Screwis British, while Dani is American. Adaptational Sexuality: InThe Turn of the Screw, the governess has feelings for the man who hired her, whileDani is a lesbian.

characters.name: Hannah
characters.description: The housekeeper of Bly Manor. Achievements in Ignorance:By simply not realizing that she has died, Hannah, unlike every other ghost at Bly, continues on with her normal routine as though nothing had happened. Cannot Spit It Out: She never manages to tell Owen how she feels about himuntil after she's dead. Dead All Along:A particularly tragic example, as she dies only moments before her first appearance in the present storyline. Given the set-up, she was actually alive for the first few minutes of the first episode, up until we actually see her. Death by Adaptation:Mrs. Grose lived throughThe Turn of the Screw, but here, Hannah isDead All Along, having been murdered by Quint moments before Dani's arrival at Bly.

characters.name: Owen
characters.description: The chef of Bly Manor. His talents far outstrip his station, and he works the job primarily to support his ailing mother, whom he lives with to care for. Canon Foreigner: There is a brief mention of there being a cook employed at Bly Manor inThe Turn of the Screw, but the cook plays no further role, so Owen is essentially an entirely new character. Due to the Dead:After learning of Hannah's death, Owen personally ensures that her body is removed from the well Peter threw her into, and subsequently cleans her body and stays with her until Hannah is laid to rest. Her Heart Will Go On: He never gets overHannah's death enough to love anyone else, but is still shown to be very professionally successful and have strong platonic relationships with the other surviving characters later in life. Mama's Boy: Heavily implied, as he takes care of his ill mother and seems very close to her.He's devastated when she dies, barely holding himself together afterwards.

characters.name: Jamie
characters.description: The groundskeeper of Bly Manor, a Northern woman with a preference for plants over people. Adaptation Expansion:The storyteller inThe Turn of the Screwwas little more than a plot device whose only real personality trait was an unrequited love for the governess. Here, Jamie is an important, fleshed-out character who was actually present at Bly Manor during the story, as well asDani's romantic interest and the love of her life. Ambiguous Criminal History: While laying out herDark and Troubled Pastto Dani, Jamie mentions that she spent a few years in prison—which was where she discovered her love for gardening—but never specifies what for. ...And That Little Girl Was Me:It's eventually revealed that the Storyteller is Jamie, discussing her own story as though she was someone else. Broken Bird: She has a tough, slightly standoffish attitude, which hides a lifetime of feeling hurt and disappointed by everyone she tried to love and having to fend for herself at a young age.

characters.name: Peter
characters.description: Henry's former valet, who embezzled from his company and fled to parts unknown a year before the start of the series. Abusive Parents:His father, whom Peter does not speak highly of to Miles, is heavily implied to have sexually abused him, while his mother did nothing to stop it and is perfectly willing to blackmail her adult son when she comes back into his life (an event which evokes a horrifiedLittle "No"from Peter, who considers reliving the memory to be "like [he's] in hell"). Adaptational Sympathy: The novel's Peter Quint was little more than a scoundrel in life who became a vague, threatening presence in death. Here, he has a fleshed out backstory and a capacity for love (toxic though it may be) that greatly humanizes him. Adaptational Villainy: InThe Turn of the Screw, Peter Quint was disreputable in life, and menacing in death, with implications that he would possess Miles.All of that is true here, but unlike the novel's Quint, Peter is a definite murderer, andhis plansfor Miles are much more explicitly sinister and self-serving. Adaptation Expansion: In the novel, Quint was aPosthumous Characterwhose ghost (assuming it truly existed) never spoke, and all information about him was relayed secondhand. Here,despite still being dead, he gets a great deal of focus and development that fleshes out his character considerably.

characters.name: Rebecca
characters.description: The former au pair of the Wingrave children, who left the position under tragic circumstances after the departure of Peter Quint. Adaptational Heroism: Miss Jessel appears to be a malevolent ghost inThe Turn of the Screw, and while it seems like Rebecca will end up that way for a while,she ultimately goes against Peter's plan to possess the kids in order to save Flora and Dani, and is even willing to relive the trauma of her own death by drowning to spare Flora having to experience that when the Lady in the Lake takes her. Adaptational Job Change: Like Dani, she was a governess inThe Turn of the Screw, while here she's specifically an au pair. Her intended career as a lawyer is also new. Adaptational Nice Guy: On top ofAdaptational Heroism, one of the few things we hear about for definite inThe Turn of the Screwis that Miss Jessel wasn't the nicest person, as it's heavily implied that she abused Miles and Flora. None of that is present here. Adaptation Expansion: Like Peter, Miss Jessel was aPosthumous CharacterinThe Turn of the Screw, and everything the reader learns about her comes secondhand. In the series, she getsa first nameand plenty of focus, resulting in a much more fleshed out character.

characters.name: Flora & Miles
characters.description: Children Are Innocent:They trust and love Peter and Rebecca and are willing, albeit with some reluctance, to go along with whatever they say, even believing Peter's claim that he won't hurt Dani (at that point bound, gagged, and clearly terrified for her and the children's lives). Peter exploits their innocence and fondness for him to manipulate them into letting him and Rebecca steal their bodies. Creepy Child: They're adapted from trope codifiers of this, after all. While Miles and Flora are both really sweet and lovely children, Dani begins to find there is something rather off about them.Subverted in that the childrenarecharming and lovely, even going so far as to attempt to protect Dani, but the spirits possessing them... Demonic Possession:The two of them spend a large part of the series (as well as before the start of the story) being possessed on and off by Rebecca and Peter, respectively. Easily Forgiven: Even before she figures out theirpossession, Dani is extremely forgiving of their creepiness. She's also very forgiving of them fortying her up and nearly killing her, knowing that they were being manipulated by Peter and Rebecca. I See Dead People: For much of the series, Miles and Flora are the only ones who can see the various ghosts haunting Bly Manor.

characters.name: Henry
characters.description: The uncle of the Wingrave children and brother of their father, now their legal guardian following the death of their parents. Adaptational Heroism: InThe Turn of the Screw, the children's uncle just couldn't be bothered to see their upbringing himself, hence his reliance on the staff at Bly and the governess. Here, while Henryseemssimilar,what actually keeps him away from the children is shame over his affair with Charlotte (which resulted in Flora) and grief over the death of his brother and the love of his life. In the end, driven by concern over the children, he goes to Bly to try and help them, and goes on to be their father figure for many years to come. Adaptational Sexuality: Possibly. It's heavily implied in "Owen Wingrave" that Owen is haunted by the soldier's ghost at night as a replacement for his own repressed homosexuality, which led to him breaking up with his fiancée. Henry is attracted to women, as evidenced byhis relationship with Charlotte. The Alcoholic: Started hitting the bottle hard after the death of his brother and his sister-in-law. CPR: Clean, Pretty, Reliable: Although he gets throttled or neck snapped by the Lady of the Lake, Owen is able to revive him pretty easily in the final episode.

characters.name: Dominic & Charlotte
characters.description: The Wingrave children's parents, who died two years earlier. Deceased Parents Are the Best: They died two years before the start of the series, and Flora and Miles miss them terribly. A Family Affair:Charlotte had been cheating on her husband with his brother. Good Parents: They were by all accounts wonderful parents, despite their marital problems. Dominic berates his brother and warns him away from Flora, reminding him that while he may have fathered her, she is his daughter alone.The crux of Peter's manipulation of the children is a promise that they can be forever reunited with their parents in memories once they've been permanently possessed. How They Treat the Help: They treated the staff at Bly Manor more like family than employees. Hannah in particular had a close friendship with Charlotte.

characters.name: In General
characters.description: And I Must Scream: If you die on the grounds of Bly Manor, you become a ghost with no way to leave, either to elsewhere in the world or to the next one. Worse,the longer a ghost remains, the more the constant looping of their own memories wears at them, gradually eroding their minds into nothing even as they must continue to exist. Not a fate anyone would want, and not one any of them sought. Barred from the Afterlife:Viola's gravity forces everyone who dies at Bly Manor to remain there as ghosts and prevents them from moving on. The curse is broken after Viola's spirit is taken into Dani's body, with only Viola herself remaining bound to Earth. The Blank: The few ghosts properly seen have faces Flora would describe as "unfinished." Most are missing all facial features save a lipless, toothless slit of a mouth. The Doll-Face Child is the only one we see with more than that, and they still have distorted, half-formed features that leave only the shape of things like eyes. Empty Shell:The oldest ghosts lose so much of themselves that they become nothing more than patterns and habits without minds. They may sing along to a song they hear, but they barely do anything more than simply exist. Freeze-Frame Bonus: Barring the Lady in the Lake, they all make appearances throughout the show hidden in the background. The Plague Doctor is the one most likely to be spotted by casual viewers due to the distinctive shape of his hat and mask being easier to spot in silhouette. The freeze frame part comes in when they appear and disappear between shots,which turns out to be a plot point; not only can ghosts choose whether or not to be visible, they flicker in and out of existence as they fall back into their own memories.

characters.name: The Man with the Shiny Glasses
characters.description: A specter that haunts Dani. He was known in life as Edmund O'Mara. Ambiguous Situation: Is he a proper ghost or something else? He is one of only two supernatural entities that didn't die at Bly Manor, andhe disappears from the show after Dani chooses to confront him, meaning he was likely less an actual ghost and more just a representation of Dani's guilt over her fiancé's death. Dogged Nice Guy:He first proposed to Dani when they were children, and then kept asking over the years until she finally said yes, because she thought that was how it was supposed to go. Incompatible Orientation:While she did truly love Eddie as a friend, Dani could never return his romantic feelings, being a lesbian. Look Both Ways:He angrily got out of his car into the street after Dani told him she couldn't marry him, and immediately got hit by a truck.

characters.name: The Doppelgänger
characters.description: A specter that haunts Henry. He looks identical to him, but with an eternally mocking, eerie smile. Allegorical Character: It is implied that he is not so much a literal ghost as much as he's the personification of Henry's alcoholism and self-loathing. Doppelgänger: After Dominic and Charlotte died, Henry began being visited by a figure looking exactly like him but always smiling smugly and who constantly berates him.It's left unclearwhether it's actually physically present or all in his head,though it does disappear once he finallyconfronts and accepts the fact that Dominic and Charlotte are really gone. Faux Affably Evil: He keeps up a jolly demeanor andwide grinwhile verbally torturing Henry over his shortcomings. My Greatest Failure: He loves to torture Henry by reminding him of all his past mistakes and failures.

characters.name: The Plague Doctor
characters.description: A figure in a plague doctor's garb, and the first ghost to be properly seen by the audience. Deathly Unmasking:Having found Viola Lloyd intruding, he took his mask off to get a better look at her - only for Viola to snap his neck. Malevolent Masked Man: He wears a mask and is an eerie specter from beyond the grave. However, he isn't actively malevolent,being the third oldest of the manor's ghosts and having lost almost all of his personality as a result. Plague Doctor: He is, or at least was, onefrom a period where Bly Manor was used to house the victims of a plague. He also averts the trend of plague doctors in sleek bird-like masks and stylish clothes, instead wearinga historically accurate mask and clothes of appropriate raggedness◊.

characters.name: The Doll-Face Child
characters.description: A child with a doll-like face. Ambiguous Gender: They have no face or voice, and their clothing and hair are gender neutral, making it impossible to tell their gender. Flora called them "he," butthe Lady in the Lake mistook them for her daughter, and even various real-world articles about the show differ on whether they call them a girl or a boy. Censored Child Death: Unlike the other known victims ofthe Lady in the Lake, whose deaths are shown on-screen and in varying detail, the child is simply shown being carriedtoward the lake, with a strong implication of what happened to them. Creepy Doll: They have this appearance, as they first show up blending in with a bunch of dolls in the basement. This is because their face is actually that of a doll's, pulled off and given to them by Flora.

characters.name: The Woman in the Attic
characters.description: A ghost who dwells exclusively in the attic of Bly Manor. She was known in life as Perdita Willoughby. Chekhov's Gunman: Even among the manor's ghosts, she appears to be pretty unimportant at first due to not popping up as much as the others. Later, it turns out she's a big reason for the existence of the Bly Manor curse. The Dog Bites Back:After years of being abused and slowly growing jealousy, Perdita smothered Viola while taking care of her. The Glorious War of Sisterly Rivalry: Averted. She and her sister were very close,until Viola became deathly ill and started abusing her for years. Green-Eyed Monster:Perdita towards Viola. So much so that the once loving relationship the sisters had begins to sour as Perdita begins to feel neglected in comparison to her beautiful, strong-willed older sister admired by everyone, coupled with Viola's own bitterness and avarice at being sick leading to her emotionally abusing Perdita, culminating with Perdita smothering Viola to death.Though an alternate interpretation might suggest that it was Viola who felt this towards Perdita. One evening, after Viola had taken ill, her husband Arthur asked Perdita to dance. Perdita initially refused but gave in, and Viola witnessed them dancing, then physically abused Perdita and accused her of trying to steal her husband. Viola's continued abuse and jealousy eventually culminated in Perdita having enough and suffocating Viola to death.

characters.name: The Lady in the Lake
characters.description: A ghost who rises up from the Bly Manor lake, regarded with fear by all who know of her. She was known in life as Viola Lloyd (née Willoughby). Adaptational Angst Upgrade: Inthe original short story, the Willoughby sisters are simply caught in a love triangle with a handsome family friend, each jealous of his affection for the other, with a living mother and brother to handle the family's affairs. Here, they are orphans living in an era when women could not legally do many of the tasks required to manage a sizable manor, fighting to maintain control over their own property and their own lives, who find themselves in a deadly tuberculosis-induced rivalry just when it looks like they've finally secured their futures and happiness. Adaptational Nice Guy: Just barely. In the original story, Viola (named Perdita; the sisters' names were reversed for the series) leaves her clothes to her daughter to keep them out of her sister's hands after her death, knowing it's the one part of her life she might be able to keep her sister from seizing from her. Here, the dresses and jewelry were genuinely extremely precious to Viola, and she leaves them to Isobel because she wanted her daughter to have the objects she had dearly loved.It's also shown that the sisters were very close and had a loving relationship before Viola's illness and descent into paranoia; in the original story, the two girls had a bitter and intense rivalry. It's also shown that the sisters were very close and had a loving relationship before Viola's illness and descent into paranoia; in the original story, the two girls had a bitter and intense rivalry. Ailment-Induced Cruelty: Viola's long, agonizing illness (made even longer and more agonizing by her refusal to die), along with her paranoia about Arthur and Perdita's relationship, made her bitter and abusive towards her sister,which eventually pushed Perdita into murdering her.
